## Introduction
Cell segmentation is the process of partitioning images into cells. Through this process, pixels are assigned to individual cells. After performing
cell segmentation features from cells can be obtained by analyzing characteristics of their assigned pixels. For example, pixel size can be
inferred by the number of pixels assigned to a single cell, or protein expression can be calculated as the average pixel intensity value for a 
specific image channel. Adequate cell segmentation is pivotal to obtain satisfactory results. 

In CSM cell segmentation is a two or three step process.

* __Obtain cell segmentation masks:__ Original images will be used to compute cell segmentation mask images. Segmentation masks are images where pixels are assigned a pixel value according to the cell they belong. Therefore there are as many unique pixel values as cells are contained in the 
image. 

* __Refine cell segmentation masks:__ If cell segmentation masks have been computed using overlapping tiled images, edge bias correction may need
to be applied. For more information, please see the Working with large images and TMAs vignette.

* __Generate the cell feature matrix:__ The original images and cell masks can be used to obtain relevant cell features.

## Test datasets

The test datasets consists of two small 500x500 pixels breast carcinoma TIFF images. They have been 
stained with a multiplexed immunofluorescence protocol for the following markers: 
"DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3". 
The original images can be found at: https://immunoatlas.org/.

```{r Images, results='hide'}
#Generate a temporary directory to place the input images
Input_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir1_Input")
dir.create(Input_Dir, recursive = TRUE)

#Save images in Input directory
purrr::map(1:2,
function(Image){
   EBImage::writeImage(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test[[Image]],
   file.path(Input_Dir, names(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test)[Image]))
})
```

## Segmentation based on watershed algorithm
CSM implements cell segmentation based on the [watershed algorithm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watershed_(image_processing) "link to Wikipedia"). Watershed-based cell segmentation
is fast and computationally efficient. However, the user should take into account that this type of algorithms are limited when it comes to identify cell boundaries in very densely 
populated areas. Watershed algorithms work best when cell morphologies are homogeneous and cells are evenly spaced.
Anyways, with adequate parameter tuning this algorithm can perform nicely with very little computational cost. CSM implements watershed-based cell segmentation thanks 
to the simpleSeg Bioconductor package.
In order to maximize the capabilities of watershed-based cell segmentation process there are several parameters that need to be carefully tuned:

* __Nuclear channels:__ The algorithm requires at least one nuclear marker. The marker must have a good signal to noise ratio and clearly delineate cell nuclei. Several nuclear markers can be
provided. If so, the algorithm will combine nuclear channels into one single image. Merging can also be performed by Principal Component Analysis (PCA).

* __Nuclear channel pre-processing:__ Nuclear channels provide the main information to perform watershed-based segmentation. If the channels containing cell nuclei information are noisy,
or nuclei show plenty of empty spaces, they will not serve their purpose. Therefore, CSM allows the user to pre-process nuclear channels to improve segmentation results. Image opening or closing can
be used to remove small noisy areas or fill holes in nuclei. In addition, the minimum and maximum pixel values can be provided as well as the gamma correction to modify the pixel value histogram.

* __Smoothening:__ Image-channels can be pre-processed to remove noise. One of the most common ways is to apply gaussian filters to smooth out contours.

* __Cell-body method:__ Once the cell nuclei have been identified the algorithm can optionally infer the cell's cytoplasm.This can be done by nuclear mask dilation (enlarging the nuclear mask by
a user defined number of pixels) or by inferring cytoplasms based on cytoplasmic markers.

* __Watershed type:__ The algorithm may identify boundaries by differences in intensity, by distance to closest background pixel or both.

* __Normalization:__ Pixel values may be pre-processed using several different approaches. In addition, background pixels can be identified by the expression pattern of certain key tissue defining 
image channels.

* __Minimum pixel value:__ If any cell identified is smaller than this user provided parameter, it will be removed from the segmentation mask.

* __Neighbor distance:__ The minimum distance (in pixels) required to keep two cells as independent objects. Small values result in higher number of cells identified.

* __Disc size:__ If cytoplasmic dilation is to be performed, the size (in pixels) of the nuclear mask dilation.

* __Tolerance:__ The minimum height of the object in the units of image intensity between its highest point (seed) and the point where it contacts another object (checked for every contact pixel).
If the height is smaller than the tolerance, the object will be combined with one of its neighbors, which is the highest.

### Segmentation tester app
In order to make the parameter tuning process easier, CSM implements a shiny App to interactively test segmentation parameters.
The function allows the user to test all the above mentioned parameters. In addition, if the user zooms in the main image panel, only the zoomed in area will be tested, speeding up the
testing process. Once the parameters are found to be adequate, the user can save the results in an object in the global environment by hitting the `Download Parameters` button.

```{r, echo=FALSE, out.width="100%"}
knitr::include_graphics("Figures/Segmentation_tester_app.png")
```


```{r app, eval = FALSE}
#Can only run interactively
Input_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir1_Input")
dir.create(Input_Dir, recursive = TRUE)

#Save images in Input directory
purrr::map(1:2,
function(Image){
   EBImage::writeImage(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test[[Image]],
   file.path(Input_Dir, names(CSM_MiniMultiTiff_test)[Image]))
})

#Launch the app------------------------------------------------------------
Watershed_tester_app(
  Directory = Input_Dir,
  Ordered_Channels = c("DAPI", "PDL1", "GZMB", "PD1", "CK-EPCAM", "CD8a", "FOXP3")
)
```

### Performing cell segmentation
Once the segmentation parameters have been tuned, the user can compute cell segmentation masks and save them in an output directory. 

```{r Segmentation, eval = FALSE}
#Get the images
Output_Dir <- tempfile(pattern = "tempdir1_Output")
dir.create(Output_Dir, recursive = TRUE)

#Check a segmentation parameters list obtained using the dedicated function----------
print(CSM_SegmentParams_test)

#Run the cell segmentation and feature extraction process (can only run interactively)--
Watershed_cell_mask_generator(
  Directory = Input_Dir,
  Output_directory = Output_Dir,
  Parameter_list = CSM_SegmentParams_test
)
```


## Obtaining cell feature data
After obtaining the segmentation masks, the next step is to obtain a cell feature matrix that can be used for subsequent analysis. This can be obtained using the `Cell_feature_extractor` function.
The function requires two basic arguments, Image_directory (path to the folder containing the original images) and Mask_directory (path to the folder containing the cell masks). 

By default, the function will return the following features for every cell:

* Image where the cell is located
* Cell id
* Cell X and Y centroid coordinates
* Basic morphology data (size, diameter, sphericity...)

If `Compute_basic_features = TRUE` argument is set, then the original images will be used to compute channel expression values. This includes:

* Average expression
* Standard deviation
* Quantiles (Optional). The quantiles to be computed are indicated using the `quantiles_to_calculate` argument. It can be set to NULL to avoid quantile computation.

If `Compute_texture_features = TRUE` argument is set, texture features will be computed for every cell and channel being analyzed. Haralick texture features are based on the GLCM wich requires a distance 
parameter to be computed. The distance is provided using the `Texture_pixel_distance` argument.

Additionally, subcellular compartments can be defined. This allows the user to compute cell features in specific cell regions (cell nuclei, cytoplasm, membrane...) as long as this subcellular
regions can be defined thresholding specific image channels to generate subcellular cell masks. Parameters to define subcellular regions can be provided through the `Subcellular_compartment_parameter_list` 
argument. This should take the form of a list of named lists. Every element of the list should contain the following items:

* Channel_name: The names of the channels that will be used for subcellular compartment definition. If various channels are providaded, they will be averaged.
* Type: Either `Positive` or `Negative`. If positive, the subcellular compartment will be defined by the pixels that are found to be above the threshold. If negative the subcellular compartment will be
defined by the pixels that are below the threshold. This can be useful to define perfectly complementary subcellular regions. For example, a Positive subcellular region based on DAPI can be used to identify
the nuclear region, while a Negative region will define the cytoplasm and membrane region.
* Threshold_type: Either Arbitrary or Otsu.
* Threshold_value: If Threshold_type is Arbitrary, the numeric value used for the threshold.
* Blurr: A logical value indicating if blurring should be performed before thresholding.
* Sigma: If blurring is required, a numeric value indicating the sigma of the blurring kernel.

```{r Feature_extraction, eval = FALSE}
#Prepare parameters to obtain subcellular nuclear and cytoplasmic compartments---
Subcellular_compartment_parameters <-
 list(Nuclear = list(Channel_name = "DAPI",
                     Type = "Positive",
                     Threshold_type = "Arbitrary",
                     Threshold_value = 0.05,
                     Blurr = TRUE,
                     Sigma = 0.4),
      Cytoplasmic = list(Channel_name = "DAPI",
                         Type = "Negative",
                         Threshold_type = "Arbitrary",
                         Threshold_value = 0.05,
                         Blurr = TRUE,
                         Sigma = 0.4)
 )

#Obtain the cell feature matrix--------------------------------------------
Cell_feature_extractor(Image_directory = Input_Dir,
                      Mask_directory = Output_Dir,
                      Ordered_Channels = CSM_SegmentParams_test[["Channels_to_keep"]],
                      Subcellular_compartment_parameter_list = Subcellular_compartment_parameters)

```

The result is a tibble containing cell features.
